title: People Who Project Their Own Flaws Onto Others
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explains psychological projection -- the tendency for people, especially insecure leaders, to accuse others of the very flaws they struggle with themselves. It offers concrete examples, such as leaders who question others' work ethic while privately battling their own discipline, and explains why this pattern distorts the value of feedback. The author gives two tells for spotting projected criticism: an accusation disproportionate to the situation, and a reaction that seems irrationally intense given the circumstances. Because genuine feedback is essential for growth, the piece argues readers need to be able to separate accurate criticism from projected noise so they know what to actually act on.
points: People with deep insecurities commonly project their own flaws onto others as criticism.
Projected feedback often shows up as accusation rather than constructive, proportionate critique.
An unexplainably intense reaction to something minor is a signature sign of projection.
Distinguishing projected criticism from accurate feedback protects growth without discarding useful input.
quotes: People with deep insecurities have a peculiar habit. They commonly project those insecurities onto others.
By attributing their own flaws to others, they avoid having to examine and deal with those deficiencies.
When a leader or colleague has an exceptionally strong reaction to something you say or do that has no basis or reasonable explanation, they are likely projecting their insecurities onto you.
In other words, whatever flaw they struggle with is often the focus of their behavior with others.
For instance, leaders who ridicule others about their lack of confidence often struggle with their own self-confidence.
Similarly, colleagues who struggle with holding themselves accountable often blame others for their lack of responsibility.
Any time a person shifts the focus from their own shortcomings onto others, they are said to be projecting .
While everyone projects now and again, people (especially leaders) with deep insecurities do so frequently, creating misinformation disguised as feedback.
